items.title: Developer reports opening 23 PRs in one day with AI agents and adjusting workflow
facts: I opened 23 PRs today on 3 different contexts, and to be honest I had to put most of my mental effort on not getting lost.
These are the changes I made to handle 2-3x the volume: Better design since the beginning, Critical PRs go to me for review, New task = new session, No coordinators past 150k tokens.

x_posts.author: @liamszefner
x_posts.text:
First time feeling genuinely overwhelmed by AI output at Opereit.

I opened 23 PRs today on 3 different contexts, and to be honest I had to put most of my mental effort on not getting lost. 

Might not sound like much given what I do on my personal side, but to keep a very high bar and review critical code and making sure other engineers can read, understand and work on top of the PRs it took a LOT of focus.

Small plus, I fried my claude 5h window twice AND bloated the slack channel ( mb team ). 

Today proved that my workflow wasn't ready to handle this volume. These are the changes I made to handle 2-3x the volume:

- Better design since the beginning: I can be wrong in the approach I take, or miss a few things, but not following conventions or allowing workers to assume things is the reason we need human reviews.

- Critical PRs: UI/UX, key features and db goes to me for a business and approach review before sending to the team  

- New task = new session: Workers don't need to remember stuff, so if we need to review / fix comments we start fresh.

- No coordinators past 150k tokens: More then this gets handed off to a new one.

- Asking for reviews by stack, not individual PRs: Sounds dumb but I think the effect will be to not bloat the channel, and for new PRs just reply in thread. 

some more as well, but less relevant ( ex: cleanup when done, workers are haiku... ) 

So to sum up, to 10x the volume I have to 10x the context awareness and 10x the tokens with a quality workflow, and keep iterating and pushing and pushing

items.title: Discussions on agent coordination and the need for isolation in multi-agent coding
facts: A coding agent picking up a task and writing to your repo needs the handoff to come with isolation, not just shared context. That's what git worktrees are for.

x_posts.author: @stretchcloud
x_posts.text:
Everyone keeps shipping a universal task layer for agents, and it says something that almost nobody is shipping it for the one agent category that actually touches production code.

Roma just launched its 2.0 version: a to-do list that creates tasks automatically and hands them to whichever agent should run them, Claude, Grok Bot, Muse, whatever you've got wired in, with shared context between them. Jan Senderek built it after selling Loom to Dropbox back in 2014, and the pitch is simple: you stopped using one agent months ago, so stop pretending your tools only understand one. 378 thousand views in a few hours says the pitch is landing.

That's the right instinct pointed at the wrong layer for anyone writing software with these things. A chat agent picking up a task from a shared queue can fail safely, worst case it gives a bad answer and you ask again. A coding agent picking up a task and writing to your repo needs the handoff to come with isolation, not just shared context. That's what git worktrees are for, and it's why Campfire runs Claude Code, Codex, Goose, Aider and OpenHands side by side in separate worktrees instead of one shared workspace, so two agents racing the same ticket never step on each other's changes, and a majority vote decides what actually merges, not one model's judgment.

The to-do list for agents is a real category now. The version of it that matters for code needs permission voting and session replay built in from day one, not bolted on after the first merge conflict.

https://github.com/stretchcloud/campfire
https://x.com/jans/status/2120546950496043111
